planner_notes: Two tasks, one per accepted finding, one wave. The claims are disjoint. Task 1 claims the orchestrator's db/queries.ts plus its test and the ui/server app plus its test. Task 2 claims daemon.ts, daemon.test.ts, cli.test.ts, docs/runbooks/ops.md and .claude/skills/bs/status.md. No file is claimed twice. daemon.ts does not import db/queries.ts or ui/server/src/app.ts, and neither of those imports daemon.ts, so there is no import edge between the tasks and no dependency edge is declared. widest = 2.

Task 2 reverses a documented design decision, on the operator's instruction in the planning brief. Today acquireLock's docblock, docs/runbooks/ops.md ('dead means the stale lock is overwritten') and the daemon.test.ts case 'takes over a lock file it cannot parse' all say an unparseable lock is taken over. After this epic an unreadable lock is refused. A torn lock left by a crash mid-write then needs a person to delete the file. A lock that parses and names a dead pid is still taken over as today. That is the common crash case, because the lock is one small write.

Task 2 keeps the D-21 watcher doctrine for the finding memory: a tick never dies over findings.json. A corrupt memory is read as empty, as today, but the tick now reports one `unreadable-state` attention finding instead of resetting in silence.

Neither task edits factory/policies/**. The new failure code `daemon.unreadable-state` is a module-scoped SmithError code in the existing `daemon.` namespace, beside `daemon.already-running`. It is not a taxonomy.yml `error:` class, because nothing in this epic appends an error-logged event. See open_questions.
open_questions: Taxonomy fit: taxonomy.yml's `error:` classes (spec, contract, execution, integration, economy, judgment, coordination, memory) have no class for 'a daemon state file exists but cannot be read'. The nearest is execution.env-failure, and it does not fit well. The plan does not need one, because the refusal is a thrown SmithError code (`daemon.unreadable-state`) and not a logged error event. If the operator wants these refusals logged as error events, a taxonomy class is an operator edit to factory/policies/taxonomy.yml, and this plan does not make it.

Recovery cost (operator confirm): once an unreadable lock is refused, `smith daemon start`, `smith daemon run` and `smith daemon stop` all refuse. The only recovery is to delete daemon.pid by hand after confirming that no daemon is using the directory. The error message and ops.md say exactly that. Giving `smith daemon stop` a force flag that clears an unreadable lock is out of scope for this epic and is not planned.

Residual, not planned: the lock is still created with a single non-atomic `wx` write. Making lock creation atomic (tmp file plus link) would shrink the torn-lock window. That is a separate change and not part of finding 442cd7f2.

tasks.objective: Epic criterion 2, finding 442cd7f2. The private `readJsonFile<T>()` in `factory/orchestrator/src/daemon.ts` (about line 946) returns null on ANY error: a failed JSON.parse, EACCES, EISDIR, all of them. It also checks `existsSync` and then reads, which is a TOCTOU. So a corrupt `daemon.pid`, `status.json` or `findings.json` looks exactly like an absent one. Replace it with a reader that separates two outcomes. ABSENT is `readFileSync` throwing ENOENT, and it still returns null. UNREADABLE is any other read error, a JSON.parse failure, or a parsed value of the wrong shape, and it throws `new DaemonError('daemon.unreadable-state', <message>, { path, reason })`. The message names the file path and the underlying reason, and says that the file exists but cannot be read, so it is not treated as absent. The shape rules: for the lock (`readLock`), a non-null object whose `pid` is a number, which also closes today's `typeof lock.pid !== 'number'` -> null masquerade; for `status.json` and `findings.json`, a non-null, non-array object. Behaviour per caller, which is the contract: (1) `readLock` returns null when absent and throws `daemon.unreadable-state` when unreadable. (2) `acquireLock`, and so `runDaemon` (`smith daemon run`, including `--once`), refuses on an unreadable lock. It propagates the throw before any tick runs, writes nothing, and leaves the lock file's bytes unchanged. A parseable lock with a dead pid is still taken over, and a parseable lock with a live pid still throws `daemon.already-running`. (3) `smith daemon start` in cli.ts already calls `readLock` before it spawns. It therefore refuses with `daemon.unreadable-state` and spawns no child, with no cli.ts edit. cli.ts is NOT claimed. (4) `daemonStatus`, and so `smith daemon status`, throws `daemon.unreadable-state` when either the lock or status.json is unreadable. The CLI's existing top-level handler prints `{"error":{"code":"daemon.unreadable-state",...}}` on stdout and exits 1. It does not print a `running:false` report, so 'no daemon' (the report, with `running:false`) and 'daemon state unreadable' (the error object) are different outputs. (5) `stopDaemon`, and so `smith daemon stop`, throws `daemon.unreadable-state` on an unreadable lock. It signals no pid and leaves the file in place, because it cannot know which process owns the lock. (6) `releaseLock` never throws: on an unreadable lock it returns false and leaves the file. It runs in runDaemon's `finally`, and a throw there would mask the loop's own outcome. (7) `readFindingMemory` returns `{}` when absent and throws `daemon.unreadable-state` when unreadable. runDaemon's per-tick memory read (`tickWithMemory`) catches exactly that code, and nothing else, and ticks with `{}` memory. It passes the failure to `runTick` through one new optional `TickOptions` field, `memoryUnreadable?: { path: string; reason: string }`. When that field is set, `runTick` emits one finding `{ kind: 'unreadable-state', severity: 'attention', sessionId: null, subject: <memory path>, detail: <reason plus the consequence: the memory was read as empty, so every standing finding is dated as new this tick> }`. It goes through the same aging and counting path as every other finding, so `attention` and `newAttention` include it. `'unreadable-state'` is added to the `FindingKind` union. The tick still completes, still writes status.json, and still rewrites findings.json with valid JSON (the D-21 watcher rule: a watchdog never dies over its own scratch file). `runTick` called without the field behaves exactly as today. Rewrite the docs that describe the old lenient behaviour: the `acquireLock` and `readFindingMemory` docblocks; docs/runbooks/ops.md, which is the lock paragraph at about line 361 ('dead means the stale lock is overwritten'), the findings.json paragraph at about line 376 ('A missing or corrupt file is read as an empty memory'), a new `unreadable-state` row in the findings table at about line 180, and one sentence in the `smith daemon status` section saying an unreadable lock or status file exits 1 with the `daemon.unreadable-state` error object instead of a report; and .claude/skills/bs/status.md step 1, which gains a fourth reading for the error object: the daemon state is unreadable, lead with it, name the path from `details.path`, and do not render it as `running: false`.

functional_clauses: One reader decides 'absent' against 'unreadable' for all three daemon state files. Absent is ENOENT from the read itself, never an `existsSync` pre-check, so a file deleted between check and read cannot throw a raw ENOENT. Unreadable is every other error, including a failed JSON.parse and a parsed value of the wrong shape. It surfaces as `DaemonError('daemon.unreadable-state', message, { path, reason })`. `reason` is the underlying error's code when it has one (for example `EACCES`), otherwise its message.

Per-caller behaviour is exactly the seven numbered rules in the objective: readLock throws; acquireLock/runDaemon refuse without ticking or writing; `smith daemon start` refuses without spawning, through its existing readLock call; daemonStatus/`smith daemon status` throw, so the CLI prints the error object and exits 1; stopDaemon throws without signalling or deleting; releaseLock returns false without throwing; readFindingMemory throws, but runDaemon ticks with `{}` and reports one `unreadable-state` attention finding.
`TickOptions` gains one optional field, `memoryUnreadable?: { path: string; reason: string }`. `FindingKind` gains `'unreadable-state'`. No existing field or member changes meaning.
A parseable lock is handled as today: a dead pid is taken over, and a live pid throws `daemon.already-running` with the existing message and details.

The error message tells the operator how to recover: confirm that no `smith daemon run` process is using this directory, then delete the named file. It must not suggest `smith daemon stop`, which refuses the same file.

Every backticked dotted code the edited docs cite must be one the source raises.
No edit to `factory/orchestrator/src/cli.ts`. The CLI's existing top-level SmithError handler is the output path. An out-of-claim need is reported to the planner as error.spec.spec-gap and not taken.
The daemon's exported functions keep their names and signatures. `daemon.ts` is imported by `cli.ts` and `findingAge.ts`.
The D-21 watcher rule holds for the finding memory: a corrupt findings.json never stops a tick.
A task worktree has no node_modules. Symlink the main clone's node_modules to run the suites, and never `git add -A` there.
